cues.text: Chapter seven: Exam consolidation.
Let's pull this session together by looking at what you need to be able to do for the exam.
There are several areas, and I'll take them in the order the source gives them.
First, learn all twelve principles.
That means all twelve, not a favourite few.
You should know each one well enough to recognise it in a scenario and explain it.
Second, learn Scrum in terms of four groups: its accountabilities, its events, its artifacts, and its commitments.
Be able to name what belongs in each group and say what each item is for.
Keep the groups separate in your mind, because exam questions often test whether you can tell an accountability from an event, or an artifact from a commitment.
Third, learn Kanban: its flow, its WIP, which stands for work in progress, and its metrics.
Know how work moves through the system, why limiting work in progress matters, and which measures are used to understand how Kanban is performing.
Fourth, be clear on iteration versus increments.
These two words are easy to blur together, but they are not the same thing.
Be ready to define each one and explain how they differ.
Fifth, understand backlog adaptation, meaning how the backlog changes and is adapted as work goes on.
Sixth, understand technical quality.
Agile approaches are not only about process and speed, and quality of the technical work matters as well.
Now an important exam skill.
When you are given a scenario, you will often need to explain the choice of Scrum or Kanban.
The source is clear on how to decide: base the choice on the actual work.
Don't pick the framework by habit or by name.
Look at what the work in the scenario really is, then justify Scrum or Kanban from that.
Finally, a note on archived questions.
The archived continuous assessment questions on model selection, question twenty-nine and question thirty-five, also concern evolving requirements.
The lesson from them is this.
When requirements are uncertain or likely to change, short feedback cycles and incremental delivery suit that uncertainty.
They let the team learn, adjust, and deliver in pieces rather than committing everything up front.
The source adds one qualification you should keep: formal controls can coexist.
Choosing short feedback cycles and incremental delivery does not mean giving up formal controls.
The two can be used together.
